{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=decision-theoretic+foundations+of+temporal+persistence+and+instrumental+convergence+of+goals+across+agent+invocations&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.21236/ada567155\", \"title\": [\"Decision-Theoretic Foundations for Multi-Agent Systems\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.21236/ada567155\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2011, 12, 23]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.21203/rs.3.rs-11137330/v1\", \"title\": [\"Designing an Ethical Framework for Multi-Agent AI Negotiation in Hospital Clinical Decision Support Systems: From Game-Theoretic Foundations to Novel Musical Chairs Coalition Convergence Game (MC3G)\"], \"abstract\": \"Abstract\\n

Agentic AI systems are increasingly deployed in hospitals clinical decision support systems (CDSS), where multiple specialized agents negotiate over patient-care recommendations. This distributed negotiation introduced as “many hands” problem: overrides, disagreements and consensus-building can become opaque, and responsibility for erroneous outcomes cannot be clearly attributed. Existing healthcare AI ethics guidance largely address single system, output facing behavior and does not formally govern internal multi-agent negotiation. This study first synthesizes nine established game theoretic and mechanism design paradigms-including Prisoner's Dilemma, Bayesian games, signaling games, principal-agent theory, Stag Hunt, repeated games, VCG style mechanism design, Shapley value, and Chicken/Hawk-Dove mapping: their applicability and limitations for ethically accountable multi-agent CDSS negotiation. Building on this synthesis, we purpose the Musical Chairs Coalition Convergence Game (MC3G), a novel coalition-based framework that governs agent negotiation with a bounded protocol clock, a reputation-weighted convergence rule, and a mandatory escalation-to-human safety valve for any agent that fails to converge. As a proof-of-concept illustration of the framework’s qualitative behaviour rather than a clinically validated evaluation, we ran a synthetic simulation, non-inferential toy simulation (four agents, 2,000 cases per condition, varying strategic agent prevalence) comparing MC3G against naïve majority voting and reputation-only baseline. In this synthetic setting MC3G showed a lower silent failure rate alongside a higher human escalation rate, converting some undetected errors into flagged reviews. This offers a formally grounded, safety-first architecture for accountable multi-agent clinical decision-making, motivating future evaluation with real agents and data.

\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-11137330/v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 9, 24]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2307/j.ctvjsf522.4\", \"title\": [\"Decision-Theoretic Foundations\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctvjsf522.4\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2013, 3, 1]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7584879\", \"title\": [\"The normative foundations of AI regulation in North America, Europe, Russia, and China: Instrumental convergence without normative convergence\"], \"abstract\": \"The global race over Artificial Intelligence (AI) has triggered a parallel competition over regulation. Major economies are competing to shape global AI governance norms and export their values either through horizontal regulations, as the European Union does, or by 'lighttouch' intervention to foster innovation, an approach favoured by the United States and the United Kingdom. This article conducts a comparative analysis of European (European Union (EU) and United Kingdom), North American (U.S. and Canada), Russian, and Chinese policies on AI. My paper aims to answer the following question: what are the normative and philosophical foundations underlying these distinctive models of AI regulation and how is geopolitical competition affecting these models? To answer this question, I survey policy and legal documents adopted between 2016 and 2026 across six jurisdictions. My corpus includes hard law, soft law, and national strategies; supplemented by officials' public declarations. The article identifies three normative traditions: rights-based tempered by utilitarianism (EU and Canada), pragmatic-utilitarian (U.S. and UK), and collectivist (Russia and China). The central empirical finding is that there has been a rhetorical convergence towards the European model between 2019 and 2023. From 2023 until 2026, geopolitical competition has produced what I term 'instrumental convergence' towards a market-based framework, despite no normative consensus. The three models increasingly share regulatory features which obscure persisting differences in underlying values. This article makes three contributions. First, I provide an extended summary of AI policies in six countries and their evolution over time. Second, I provide a normative typology of the major AI regulatory models beyond legal instruments. Third, I document rhetorical and instrumental convergences in AI regulations, advancing hypotheses for this phenomenon. This paper aims to provide insights for policymakers and for the design of multilateral AI governance frameworks, such as those developed within the ITU, at UNESCO or the OECD. I conclude by arguing in favour of a regime of international treaties over technical harmonisation (ISO and other norms) to solve cooperation issues amid conflicting normative models. Report on AI use: Artificial intelligence tools were used at various stages of the research, such as when searching institutional literature. claims.statement: WAKE enforces a strict separation between model proposal generation and governance-based validation, preventing the model from modifying its own operational rules.

support.explanation: The governance source code explicitly states that the model cannot waive requirements or edit rules during an invocation, establishing it as a rigid authority.
support.passage: A model cannot persuade this module, reinterpret its instructions, waive a requirement, or edit the rules during an invocation.

review.alternative: The collector and governance could be tightly coupled, but are currently separated to maintain testing modularity.
review.would_change_mind: Source code indicating that the collector can inject logic directly into the governance module without proposal-state validation.

claims.statement: The collector acts as an untrusted evidence-gathering subsystem, where retrieval success or failure is recorded as durable state rather than an immediate instruction to the model.

support.explanation: The collector is defined as a boundary where model requests are merely questions, not instructions, ensuring evidence is treated as observational material.
support.passage: Model-authored research requests are questions, not evidence. This layer retrieves bounded external material and records collection outcomes so later synthesis can cite independently acquired sources.

actions.findings:
WAKE enforces a strict separation between model proposal generation and governance-based validation, preventing the model from modifying its own operational rules. [source-3aa8b30c4f8a45ce]

The collector acts as an untrusted evidence-gathering subsystem, where retrieval success or failure is recorded as durable state rather than an immediate instruction to the model. [source-add29d9603c34309]
actions.limitations: The current analysis relies on the provided source snapshots; future updates to the governance module could introduce subtle complexities in state transition that are not captured here.
actions.next_questions: How does the system handle conflicting evidence retrieved by the collector, and can the governance module independently adjudicate such conflicts without human oversight?
actions.reason: The architecture is fundamental to WAKE's operation and explains how it maintains consistency across cycles.
actions.summary: WAKE implements a 'Governance-as-Code' model, separating proposal generation (AI actor) from validation (Governance layer). The AI acts as an untrusted proposal engine, while the Governance layer serves as the immutable state manager, mirroring principles of secure, deterministic systems design. This structure ensures that no matter how complex the AI reasoning becomes, it cannot circumvent the underlying validation rules defined for research integrity and state updates.
